E1751.summary: In Atwood's Appendix, the lowest of man's lives, in which fallen man now is; it moves with the creative Essence and is to be raised through the medial life.
E1751.body: Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), calls this the lowest of man's lives: “Man is fallen; he is in the third or lowest life” [APP ¶35]. It is “that third life which moves in and with the creative Essence” [APP ¶3]. The records also say that the magic of the self-will exploits its release, that it is reached from present life through the clairvoyant life by repeated fermentation, that it is to be raised through the medial life, and that the seeker in it shows the Golden Fleece. By the order of APP ¶32–35 it apparently corresponds to the Infernal (lumbar, voluntary) life, but the text does not state this identity.

E1752.summary: In Boehme's language, as Atwood uses it, the sidereal and elementary birth: the medium of perceiving the First, which lies hidden in its mineral life.
E1752.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood uses Boehme's term: “the Third Principle, i.e., the sidereal and elementary birth, to use Boehme’s language” [APP ¶27]. It “is the medium of perceiving the First, which is hidden in its mineral life” [APP ¶27], and that life is full of defilement and temptation. Earlier Atwood also speaks of the circulation being carried upward “through a Third principle for reprobation” [IV.2 ¶20], instead of the Duad generating directly. The text does not identify it further there, and does not say whether this is the same Third Principle.

E1753.summary: In Eudoxus's account, the operation of the Fifth Key: fermentation with the Perfect Body, which makes the medicine of the Third order.
E1753.body: Eudoxus, quoted, connects the Third work with the Fifth Key: fermentation with the Perfect Body, which makes the medicine of the Third order. He declines to describe it: “I will say nothing in particular of the operation of the Third work” [IV.3 ¶14].

E1754.summary: The finished product of the work, endued with a magnetical virtue that draws divine increase; also called the terrestrial or Microcosmic Sun and the Stone of Fire.
E1754.body: The finished product: “this gold is endued with a magnetical virtue” [II.1 ¶25] that draws divine increase. The passage gives it other names: “Whence it has been called likewise the terrestrial or Microcosmic Sun, the triumphal Chariot of Antimony” [II.1 ¶25], and “this is the Stone of Fire seen in bright lines” [II.1 ¶25]. The text does not make clear whether Atwood or the source she follows is speaking.

E1755.summary: A Latin sentence that Norton's verse tells the reader to follow; the text does not say where it comes from.
E1755.body: Inside the Norton verse quoted at III.4 ¶17, “this holi letter” is the sentence to follow: “Attingens a fine usque ad finem fortiter, Disponens omnia suaviter;” [III.4 ¶17] (our rendering: reaching mightily from end to end, ordering all things sweetly). The text does not say who wrote the sentence.

E1756.summary: In the Zohar passage Atwood quotes, the Principle of all that is: unknown and shut up in itself at first, then developing and emanating Light; God's creative Thought inverts human thought.
E1756.body: The Rabbi in the Zohar, as Atwood quotes him, says: “Thought is the Principle of all that is; but it is as first Unknown and shut up in itself.” [III.3 ¶78]. It develops into Spirit or Intelligence, as “Thought emanating Light” [III.3 ¶79]. Atwood, apparently agreeing, adds that “the Thought which is of God creative is the inversion of our thought” [III.3 ¶78].

E1757.summary: In Eudoxus's account, the domains of Nature whose principles and operations the seeker must know.
E1757.body: Eudoxus, quoted, says the seeker must know “the operations of Nature in the Three Kinds” [IV.2 ¶4]. The records note that the 'three reigns' of Nature at IV.2 ¶3 may be comparable. The text does not name the Kinds here.

E1758.summary: Three domains of nature, which Atwood does not name in these passages; Hermes reputedly found their quintessential perfectibility in their homogeneal unity, and the torch diffuses life through them.
E1758.body: Atwood reports that Hermes discovered “the quintessential perfectibility of the three kingdoms in their homogeneal unity” [I.1 ¶6]. Later she says the torch diffuses energy, life and joy “in either if the three kingdoms, as we have shown, by its voluntary assimilation” [IV.4 ¶32], pointing back to an earlier proof. Neither passage names the three. The 'threefold enchantment' entry gives them as animal, vegetable and mineral [IV.4 ¶4].

E1759.summary: The principles of the work: Life resolves into them in the philosophic fermentation (Van Helmont's Salt, Sulphur and Mercury), and they are separated and reunited to produce the tincture.
E1759.body: In the passage quoting Boehme, “The same Three Principles gradually assume a new life” [II.1 ¶24]. They act in harmony to produce first whiteness and then the tincture, and Boehme speaks of “the mechanical part of the Three Principles” [II.1 ¶25]. Atwood says Life in the philosophic fermentation is “resolved into these three principles, which Van Helmont also calls Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury” [III.2 ¶28]. The author of The Triumph, quoted, speaks of “the separation and the reunion of the Three Principles” [IV.2 ¶6] without naming them. A separate set of three principles (attraction, repulsion, circulation) appears at II.1 ¶18; see that entry. The text does not say whether these are the same.

E1760.summary: The three principles of motion: attraction, repulsion as its reaction, and circulation arising from their conflict; equilibrium gives a circle, predominance an ellipse.
E1760.body: Attraction is the occult first principle of motion, and repulsion is its reaction. “Circulation is the third principle, proceeding from the conflict of the former two” [II.1 ¶18], and it mediates between them. When the two are in equilibrium the motion is a circle; when one predominates it is an ellipse. The text does not make clear whether Atwood or a source is speaking. On bringing the three into equilibrium, see 'threefold secret' [III.3 ¶9].

E1761.summary: The worlds Boehme says he knew and saw in himself; the printed passage names the divine angelical or paradisiacal world and the dark world.
E1761.body: Boehme, quoted: “I knew and saw in myself all the Three Worlds, viz., first, the divine angelical, or paradisiacal; and then the dark world” [III.2 ¶16]. As printed, the passage does not clearly name the third world.

E1762.summary: Atwood's term for how the animal, vegetable and mineral kingdoms are bound together in man's natural Identity; only the animal is developed to consciousness.
E1762.body: Atwood says man's animal, vegetable and mineral kingdoms are “bound together in the threefold enchantment of his natural Identity” [IV.4 ¶4]. Only the animal is developed to consciousness.

E1763.summary: The law under which catholic nature necessarily proceeds; its ingress, egress and alternating action make up all the phenomena of the process.
E1763.body: Atwood says that nature “operates her proper progress necessitously under the threefold law of life” [I.3 n35]. The ingress, egress and alternating action of this law make up all the phenomena of the process.

E1764.summary: In Atwood's Appendix, our life as threefold (sensuous, medial and divine), whose active, passive and resultant principles must each be evolved separately.
E1764.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood writes: “Our life is threefold.” [APP ¶182]. The three are the sensuous, medial and divine lives, and each has its key and its representative. “Each principle of the life --- active, passive, and resultant --- must be produced or evolved separately” [APP ¶183].

E1765.summary: The secret of the Art that brings attraction, repulsion and circulation into equilibrium in the ethereal bond.
E1765.body: Atwood: “great care and diligence is needed at this juncture to apply the threefold secret of the Art” [III.3 ¶9]. In context the secret apparently means bringing attraction, repulsion and circulation into equilibrium in the ethereal bond. See 'Three Principles (attraction, repulsion, circulation)'.

E1766.summary: That in which Prometheus is fabled to have hidden the stolen fire; Atwood uses 'thrysus bearers' for those who have and perceive the fire but cannot draw it forth.
E1766.body: Atwood: “For, in the thrysus, Prometheus is fabled to have concealed the fire he stole from heaven” [II.4 ¶54]. The 'thrysus bearers' are those who “had the fire indeed, and were able even to perceive it, who were without the power to discover and draw it forth to manifestation” [II.4 ¶54]. She sets them against the 'Bacchic souls'.

E1767.summary: Cited by Atwood as naming a certain earth as the principle, the most ancient element.
E1767.body: Atwood cites Timaeus as one who “mentions a certain earth as antecedent, and the most ancient element” [III.2 ¶35]. She uses this to illustrate a certain earth taken as the principle.

E1768.summary: The colouring, transmuting virtue of the work, or what carries it: the red, living soul drawn from the body, which turns imperfect bodies into gold and serves as the medicine of men and metals.
E1768.body:
**Transmuting product.** Paracelsus, quoted, calls it “Our tincture of gold” [I.1 ¶76]: a heavy red powder with an astral fire that turns imperfect metals into gold better than mined gold, and that is also medicinal. He gives “a true sign of the tincture of the philosophers” [I.1 ¶76]. Atwood describes the tinging power that transmutes imperfect bodies as ending as “a most pure and rubicund tincture of the color of flesh and blood” [I.3 n42]: “our tincture is of blood coagulated, which blood is the boundary or satisfaction of hearts” [I.3 n42]. In the Boehme and Basil Valentine passages it is “a brilliant yellow, red, or purpling tincture” [II.1 ¶24], and “this true tincture of Antimony, which is the medicine of men and metals” [II.1 ¶25]. The Christian philosophers Atwood quotes name as their chief treasure “a certain exalted tincture with which the world, if it served God and were worthy of such gifts, might be tinged and turned into most pure gold” [II.3 ¶33].

**Soul of the body.** In the Hermes material, which Atwood glosses, it is the soul drawn out by the death of the first life: “whence the soul is ediced; which is also the red and living tincture taken from the body” [I.3 n12]. In the end it is “that tincture of many dyes which, being dissolved renews itself, and dying survives itself” [I.3 n18]. Its blackness turns “into the true red” [I.3 ¶43]. The ferment “holds the tincture lest it should fly” [I.3 ¶58], and the quintessence “becomes golden and aurific, communicating its tincture” [I.3 n63].

**Boehme's Tincture.** Boehme, quoted, calls it “a Substance like water which yet is no water, but such a spirit or property: but it burns more like a kindred oil, and is called by many the Tincture” [III.2 ¶16]. He also writes: “this Tincture is the source of the material world, and gives to all essences virtue to grow” [III.2 ¶16], and “it is the most hidden thing, and also the most manifest” [III.2 ¶16]. It arises in the light: “It cometh forth from anguish into the meekness of the light” [III.3 ¶24], and its thin water-form “is water, which is the desiring tincture” [III.3 ¶24].

**Atwood's own uses.** Metals must have “their tincture set free in the subtle Origin of all life” [I.2 ¶49]. The philosopher's Mercury is “communicative of tincture” [III.3 ¶32]. Spiritual fermentation multiplies tinctures, while common gold and silver “are not tinctures, but gross compacted bodies” [IV.3 ¶21].

**Other voices.** In Norton's verse the word first means the colouring of glass [I.1 ¶52]. It is also “the tincture of holi Alkimy” [III.4 ¶10], and “He that would seek Tincture most specious Must needly avoid all things wild and vicious.” [IV.1 ¶49; cf. IV.1 ¶16]. In Eirenaeus's verse it is a tincture “of silver fine” [III.3 ¶68]. The Master says of the Son-King: “Then is he transformed in his Tincture.” [IV.2 ¶14]; he takes it from the fire and death and becomes 'of tincture super-excellent'. Eudoxus speaks of “the two mercuries which contain the two tinctures” [IV.3 ¶10] and says the Alcahest increases the metals' tincture. The theosophist describes the dark Mercury as “tinctured” by light and love, so that death becomes triumphing life [IV.3 ¶38]. For the Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine, see that entry.

E1769.summary: In Eirenaeus's account, what the first water partly extracts from the body, taken as a sign.
E1769.body: Eirenaeus, quoted, says that the first water “extracted partly the tincture of Sol” [III.1 ¶14] from the body, and treats this as a sign. The records also note that 'Tincture' is elsewhere a name for Reason, and 'foreign tincture' what Reason grinds out of the inferior life.

E1770.summary: Atwood's name for the cleansed, prepared medial receptacle of the newborn light; elsewhere, the Light from the Archaeus that comes forth as a dry splendour, identified with the Subtendent.
E1770.body: Atwood gives two related identifications. First, it is “the cleansed Augean, the already prepared medial receptacle of the newborn light” [II.4 ¶9]. Second, the Light from the Archaeus “comes forth as a dry splendour, surviving through all. And this is that Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine” [III.3 ¶71]. The same passage equates it with the Subtendent: “this is that Tincture of the Sapphiric Mine before alluded to, and that Subtendent” [III.3 ¶71]. One passage names a receptacle and the other a light, and the text does not reconcile the two.

E1771.summary: Atwood's name for the putrefying stage of the matter, a stronger poison.
E1771.body: Atwood says the matter, “which putrefying, becomes a stronger poison, and their venomous toad” [I.2 ¶40]. 'Toad' thus names the putrefying stage.

E1772.summary: The ancient book whose counsel Atwood cites to support the adepts' practice of keeping the king's secret close while revealing in part.
E1772.body: Atwood cites the book of Tobit for the adepts' concealment of 'the king': it is “to be honorable to reveal the works of the Lord; but good t keep close the secret of a king” [II.1 ¶7]. She endorses this counsel and says she keeps within 'the prophet’s advice' while revealing only in part.

E1773.summary: The Golden Treatise ascribed to Hermes Trismegistus, which Atwood cites for the physical ground and practical method of alchemy and repeatedly uses for chapter mottoes and supporting passages.
E1773.body: Atwood cites it as the Hermetis Trismegisti Tractatus Aureus de Lapidis physici secreto, in seven chapters. She uses it for the physical ground and practical method of alchemy [I.1 ¶7, I.1 n10]. She takes chapter mottoes from it: “Opus vobuscum et apud est, quod intus arripens et permanens in terra vel in mare habere potes.” [II.1 ¶2] (our rendering: roughly, the work is with you and among you, and taking hold of it within you can have it). She also uses “Naturam in primisimitabere in arte, magister.” [III.1 ¶1] (our rendering: first imitate Nature in the art, master). On our tentative rendering of the corrupt Latin of this second motto (not the book's), outer fire only excites, and an inner ethereal agent perfects all. She cites it for the 'Our Mercury' passage: “Our Mercury is philosophic, fiery, vital” [II.1 ¶12, II.1 n10]. She cites the Scholium in support of her view that external fire alters while internal fire perfects: “Que l’art imite la nature” [III.1 ¶42, III.1 n46] (our rendering: that art imitates nature). From cap. 4, “Protégé me et protegam te” [III.1 ¶44, III.1 n48] (our rendering: protect me and I will protect you) illustrates the mutual relation of Sun and Moon; the text does not name the speaker. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood says the author of the Golden Treatise seems to intermix the steps because he describes different repetitions of the fermentative process [APP ¶17].

E1774.summary: Ancient mythological tradition, which Atwood reads as commemorating spectacles of the soul's liberation that Wisdom instituted and art makes natural.
E1774.body: Atwood treats myths as spectacles of the soul's liberation that art makes natural. Her examples are the Salamander, Aeneas in Numitius, Pactolus and Midas, Medea and Jason, the Hesperides, Atalanta, Hercules and the Phoenix: “Such are a very few of the games and choice spectacles which tradition commemorates as instituted by Wisdom” [III.1 ¶70].

E1775.summary: The mesmeric state, which some writers suggest reveals the temple mysteries; Atwood treats it as a key not yet carried beyond therapy.
E1775.body: Atwood reports that some writers “suggest their Trance and its phenomena as a revelation of the temple mysteries” [II.2 ¶6]. She treats the mesmeric trance as a key that has not yet been carried beyond therapeutic use.

E1776.summary: The final passage for which contemplation of the indwelling Unity is the last preparation; its theurgic rite involves burying the body except the head.
E1776.body: Atwood calls contemplation of the indwelling Unity “the final preparative to translation” [II.4 ¶40]. She speaks of “the theurgic mandates for this translation” [II.4 ¶40], whose rite involves burying the body except the head. Compare 'translation of the consciousness' [APP ¶83].

E1777.summary: Atwood's later definition of the whole mystery: consciousness, now drawn out to sense, is thrown backwards and upwards into its First Source.
E1777.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood writes: “The whole of this mystery is a translation of the consciousness” [APP ¶83]. She explains that consciousness, now drawn out to sense, is thrown backwards and upwards into its First Source.

E1778.summary: The conversion of metals into gold or silver; Atwood traces its possibility to a universal subject and reads it as life attracted into the Stone's light, and the Adept equates it with salvation.
E1778.body:
**Historical sense.** Atwood uses the word in its historical sense: the conversion of a metal into gold or silver. Rhasis practised it publicly (“on account of the practical displays he made of his transmuting skill” [I.1 ¶34]), and she reports that Avicenna did too. Of another practitioner she writes that “there is reason to believe that he practiced transmutation” [I.1 ¶66]. Parliament and papal bulls forbade it, “forbidding transmutation, on pain of death, and the pursuit of alchemy” [I.1 ¶55]. Aquinas, quoted, holds that “Metals can be transmuted one into another, since they are of one and the same matter” [I.1 ¶42]. He adds that it must be done “transmutare metalla scilicet imperfecta secundum veritatem et non sophistice” [I.1 n50] (our rendering: to transmute, that is, imperfect metals, truly and not by trickery).

**Atwood's theory.** Atwood sets out to investigate “the theoretic ground and matter on which the physical possibility of transmutation rests” [I.1 ¶86]. She explains how the Stone acts: it “transmutes, i.e., attracts the same away from other forms into intimate coalescence with its own assimilative light” [I.2 ¶48]. The adepts, she says, have shown “the principle of Transmutation” to be “relating not to Species but to their Universal Subject” [IV.4 ¶2].

**Salvation.** The Adept, quoted, says: “Salvation is nothing else but a Transmutation” [IV.2 ¶18]. Atwood completes the statement herself: a transmutation “of the component principles of life in the circulation” [IV.2 ¶18].

E1779.summary: The ray of Light made concrete in life when it is dominant in the circulatory system; Atwood identifies it with the Philosophic Stone.
E1779.body: Atwood says the ray of Light, made concrete in life and dominant in the circulatory system, “is the transmutative ferment --- even the Philosophic Stone” [IV.4 ¶9].

E1780.summary: In Atwood's Appendix, the line contrary to the Divine (perpendicular) line; it restores to sense, and the two together form a cross.
E1780.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) Atwood sets the transverse line against the Divine line: it restores to sense: “the transverse line is the contrary; the two united form a cross +” [APP ¶13].
